FASTER?: Nth highest salary: correlated subquery (COUNT DISTINCT) vs DENSE_RANK()
column2:
Winner: DENSE_RANK() window function.

Why: The correlated subquery re-scans the table for each outer row (about O(n²)). The window version scans once and sorts once.

-- slow
SELECT DISTINCT e1.sal FROM emp e1
WHERE :n-1 = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.sal) FROM emp e2 WHERE e2.sal > e1.sal);
-- fast
SELECT sal FROM (SELECT sal, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY sal DESC) r FROM emp) WHERE r = :n;


Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Find duplicates: self-join vs GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
column2:
Winner: GROUP BY / HAVING.

Why: One scan plus a hash/sort aggregate. A self-join compares rows pairwise and multiplies row counts, producing duplicate pairs you then have to de-duplicate.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Running total: correlated subquery / self-join vs SUM() OVER (ORDER BY ...)
column2:
Winner: SUM() OVER with an explicit ROWS frame.

Why: Window runs in a single ordered pass. Self-join / correlated subquery re-reads all earlier rows for every row (quadratic). Explicit ROWS also avoids the slower default RANGE frame handling of ties.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Previous-row comparison: self-join on id-1 vs LAG()
column2:
Winner: LAG().

Why: Single scan, no join. The self-join approach also breaks when ids have gaps, so LAG is both faster and more correct.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Rows in A with no match in B: NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS vs LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL
column2:
Winner: NOT EXISTS (or LEFT JOIN IS NULL) in most cases.

Why: Both become an anti-join, and NOT EXISTS stops at the first match. NOT IN is a semantic trap: if B's column has any NULL it returns zero rows, and the optimizer may be unable to use an anti-join unless the column is NOT NULL.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Does a match exist: JOIN + DISTINCT vs EXISTS
column2:
Winner: EXISTS (semi-join).

Why: EXISTS stops at the first matching row and never multiplies rows. JOIN + DISTINCT builds the full join result and then pays for a sort/hash to remove duplicates. DISTINCT is often a sign of a bad join.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: IN (subquery) vs EXISTS
column2:
Winner: Usually a tie in modern Oracle.

Why: The optimizer transforms both into a semi-join. EXISTS is safer when the inner side is big and indexed on the correlation column; IN is fine for small lists. NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS is the case where the choice really matters (NULLs).

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Filter on a DATE column: TRUNC(dt) = DATE '2026-01-01' vs a half-open range
column2:
Winner: Range: dt >= DATE '2026-01-01' AND dt < DATE '2026-01-02'.

Why: A function on the column makes the predicate non-sargable, so a normal index on dt can't be used (full scan). A range on the raw column allows an index range scan. Alternative: a function-based index on TRUNC(dt).

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Case-insensitive search: WHERE UPPER(name) = 'RAVI' vs WHERE name = 'Ravi'
column2:
Winner: Depends: plain predicate uses the normal index; UPPER() needs a function-based index.

Why: UPPER(name) cannot use an index on name. Fix: CREATE INDEX ix ON t (UPPER(name)). Then the UPPER query is index-eligible and fast.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: LIKE 'abc%' vs LIKE '%abc'
column2:
Winner: LIKE 'abc%'.

Why: A fixed prefix lets the B-tree do a range scan. A leading wildcard forces a full scan (the sort order of the index doesn't help). For true substring search consider Oracle Text.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Join then aggregate vs aggregate then join (big fact table, small dimension)
column2:
Winner: Aggregate the big table first, then join to the small result.

Why: Grouping before the join shrinks millions of rows to a few thousand, so the join handles far less data. Joining first drags every detail row through the join. Oracle may do this automatically (view merging / group-by placement), but writing it explicitly is safer.

SELECT d.name, a.total
FROM (SELECT dept_id, SUM(sal) total FROM emp GROUP BY dept_id) a
JOIN dept d ON d.id = a.dept_id;


Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: WHERE vs HAVING for a non-aggregate condition
column2:
Winner: WHERE.

Why: WHERE filters rows before grouping, so less data is grouped. HAVING filters after. (Oracle's optimizer can often push it down, but don't rely on it.) Use HAVING only for aggregate conditions.

-- better
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM emp WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' GROUP BY dept_id;
-- worse
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept_id, status HAVING status = 'ACTIVE';


Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: UNION vs UNION ALL
column2:
Winner: UNION ALL.

Why: UNION must sort/hash the combined rows to remove duplicates. UNION ALL just appends. Use UNION only if duplicates are possible and unwanted.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Several scalar subqueries on the same table vs one query with conditional aggregation
column2:
Winner: One pass with CASE inside the aggregate.

Why: Each scalar subquery is a separate scan. Conditional aggregation reads the table once.

-- slow: 3 scans
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status='NEW'),
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status='SHIPPED'),
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status='CANCELLED') FROM dual;
-- fast: 1 scan
SELECT COUNT(CASE WHEN status='NEW' THEN 1 END),
       COUNT(CASE WHEN status='SHIPPED' THEN 1 END),
       COUNT(CASE WHEN status='CANCELLED' THEN 1 END) FROM orders;


Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Scalar subquery in SELECT list vs JOIN
column2:
Winner: JOIN (usually).

Why: A correlated scalar subquery can run once per row returned (Oracle's scalar subquery caching helps only when few distinct inputs). A join lets the optimizer pick hash join and process in bulk.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(1) vs COUNT(col)
column2:
Winner: COUNT(*) and COUNT(1) are identical; COUNT(col) is not the same query.

Why: COUNT(*) / COUNT(1) count rows, and Oracle can use the smallest index to do it. COUNT(col) must skip NULLs, so it can't use an index unless col is NOT NULL, and it returns a different result when NULLs exist.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: SELECT * vs selecting only needed columns
column2:
Winner: Only needed columns.

Why: Less I/O and network transfer. If all needed columns are in an index, Oracle can answer from the index alone (INDEX FAST FULL / RANGE SCAN without TABLE ACCESS BY ROWID, a covering index). SELECT * also breaks when the schema changes.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Comparing a VARCHAR2 column to a number: WHERE phone = 9876543210 vs WHERE phone = '9876543210'
column2:
Winner: String literal matching the column type.

Why: With a number, Oracle implicitly applies TO_NUMBER(phone) to every row, which disables the index on phone and can even throw ORA-01722 on non-numeric values. Always match literal types to column types.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Index vs full table scan when a query returns a large share of rows (say 30%)
column2:
Winner: Full table scan.

Why: An index lookup needs a random single-block read per row. Past roughly 5-20% of rows (depends on clustering factor) multiblock sequential reads of the whole table are cheaper. Indexes win for selective filters.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Hash join vs nested loops: which is faster?
column2:
Winner: Nested loops for a small driving set + indexed inner lookup; hash join for large unsorted sets.

Why: Nested loops does a probe per outer row (great for few rows, terrible for millions). Hash join builds an in-memory hash table once and scans the other side once (needs equality joins and memory).

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Composite index (a, b): which query uses it well?  WHERE a=1 AND b=2  vs  WHERE b=2
column2:
Winner: WHERE a=1 AND b=2 (and WHERE a=1).

Why: Leftmost prefix rule: the index is sorted by a, then b. Filtering only on b can't seek into it (Oracle may use an index skip scan if a has very few distinct values). Put the most commonly filtered, equality column first.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Update/insert millions of rows: row-by-row PL/SQL loop with COMMIT each time vs single set-based SQL
column2:
Winner: Single set-based statement (or BULK COLLECT + FORALL if procedural logic is required).

Why: A loop causes a context switch between the PL/SQL and SQL engines per row, plus frequent commits (log file sync waits). One SQL statement does the work in bulk. For loads, INSERT /*+ APPEND */ uses direct-path write.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Remove all rows from a huge table: DELETE vs TRUNCATE
column2:
Winner: TRUNCATE (if you need all rows gone and no rollback).

Why: DELETE writes undo and redo for every row and fires triggers. TRUNCATE is DDL: it resets the high-water mark, generates minimal undo/redo, and can't be rolled back. For deleting most rows but keeping some, consider CTAS the rows you keep, then swap.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Same query run 10,000 times with different values: literals vs bind variables
column2:
Winner: Bind variables.

Why: With literals every statement is a new SQL text, forcing a hard parse (CPU, shared pool pressure, latch contention). Binds reuse one cached plan (soft parse). Also prevents SQL injection.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).

column1: FASTER?: Top 10 rows by salary: sort whole table vs index on salary
column2:
Winner: Index on salary: Oracle reads the index in order and stops after 10 (COUNT STOPKEY).

Why: Without an index it must sort all rows (though Oracle uses a top-N heap sort rather than a full sort). FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY vs ROWNUM <= 10 in a sorted subquery: essentially the same plan; 12c+ rewrites FETCH FIRST internally.

Verify: EXPLAIN PLAN + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY (compare cost, rows, access paths).
